Answers to Questions: Case 3
1. What is the most common etiology for pediatric lead exposure in the United States?
No safe or acceptable blood lead level (BLL) in children has been identified. Despite significant 
progress over the past four decades in reducing the prevalence of lead exposure, according to the 
Centers for Disease and Prevention (CDC) more than half a million American children between 
1 and 5 years old are estimated to have BLLs more than 5 µg/dL. The CDC states that poisoning, 
which causes learning and behavioral problems and organ damage, affects one in 38 young chil­
dren. The source of lead exposure varies depending on the region and historic and cultural back­
ground. There are three main lead source classifications: environmental, occupational, and 
miscellaneous.
